newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban halt Masood, mull Dostum cease-fire plan.
newsitem.headline: Taleban halt Masood, mull Dostum cease-fire plan.

text.p: Taleban forces have blunted an advance towards Kabul by troops loyal to ousted Afghan military chief Ahmad Shah Masood.

Masood's forces, which on Sunday heralded their final assault on the Taleban-held capital with a volley of rockets into its airport, were rolled back in the late afternoon by the purist Islamic militia, witnesses said.

Also on Sunday, Pakistani Interior Minister Naseerullah Babar conveyed a ceasefire offer from Uzbek leader General Abdul Rashid Dostum to Taleban leaders at the Islamic movement's headquarters in the southern city of Kandahar, Taleban sources in Pakistan said.
Babar, who had earlier flown from Islamabad to Dostum's base in the northern city of Mazar-i-Sharif, told them Dostum had proposed a ceasefire to take effect at noon on Monday.
"We are thinking about it," one Taleban official, Mullah Abdul Jalil, told a correspondent of the Pakistan-based Afghan Islamic Press Agency in Kandahar.

It was not immediately clear if the Uzbek leader had offered a ceasefire only on his own behalf, or if he spoke also for his partners in a defence pact signed last week -- Masood's Tajik forces and Shi'ite Moslem Hezb-i-Wahdat faction leader Karim Khalili.

Earlier in the day, building on a series of successes which brought them within rocket range of the much fought-over capital, Masood's men had captured Hussein Kot, a village on the main road south to Kabul, only 20 km (12 miles) from the city.

Shortly after taking the village, Masood's forces had loosed a fusillade of rockets into the perimeter of Kabul's airport where the Taleban, who took the capital three weeks ago, base part of their air force.
The attack caused civilian and military aircraft to immediately take off.
Later, Masood's forces, fired by the battle cry "God is greatest", advanced another two kilometers (one mile) closer to Kabul.
But the Taleban counterattacked, driving Masood's men back with a withering barrage of mortar, rocket and artillery fire, witnesses said.
By dusk a fierce battle was under way just to the north of the village, which was again under Taleban control.
Masood spokesman Mirabuddin Astana told reporters Dostum's forces were pushing down a parallel road to Kabul and were about 30 km (18 miles) from the city.
But travellers said later there did not appear to have been any significant change in the front line on that road.

Masood officer Shirin Agha told reporters troops also were streaming south to reinforce those fighting for Hussein Kot, as Masood sought to sustain the counter-offensive which has brought him from the Pansjher valley, 90 km (60 miles) to the north, to within reach of Kabul in little more than a week.
Masood's latest breakthrough came on Friday when, with the backing of Dostum's artillery, he took Bagram airbase some 50 km (30 miles) north of Kabul.
Since then he has pushed another 25 km (16 miles) south along the main road in heavy fighting and some of the few people allowed to travel to Kabul from the area report many civilian casualties.
